topics.name: Work Done by a Constant and a Variable Force
topics.summary: Work is done when a force acts on a body that undergoes a displacement. For a constant force it is the dot product \(W=\vec F\cdot\vec d=Fd\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between the force and the displacement. Work is a scalar, but it carries a sign. It is positive when \(\theta<90^\circ\) (a push along the motion), zero when \(\theta=90^\circ\), and negative when \(\theta>90^\circ\). So the normal force, the tension on a body in circular motion, and gravity during purely horizontal motion do no work however large they are, while friction and gravity on a rising body do negative work. When several forces act, find the work of each one separately using its own angle. For a force that changes with position, the work equals the area under the force-versus-displacement graph, with any area below the axis counted as negative. For a spring-type force \(F=kx\) the graph is a straight line, so the work from \(x_1\) to \(x_2\) is \(\tfrac12k\left(x_2^2-x_1^2\right)\). The SI unit of work is the joule, equal to one newton metre.
topics.worked_example:
A block is pulled 10 m along a rough floor by a 50 N force at \(53^\circ\) above the horizontal (\(\cos53^\circ=0.6\)); friction is 10 N.

Pull: \(W=50\times10\times0.6=300\) J.

Friction: \(W=10\times10\times\cos180^\circ=-100\) J.

Normal force and gravity: \(\theta=90^\circ\), so \(W=0\).

Total work \(=300-100=200\) J.
common_mistakes: Treating the work of an opposing force (friction, or gravity during lifting) as positive instead of negative.
Thinking work is zero only when the force is zero, and missing the perpendicular case \(\theta=90^\circ\).
Using the full force \(F\) instead of the component \(F\cos\theta\), or using \(\sin\theta\) in place of \(\cos\theta\).
Multiplying the final value of a variable force by the distance instead of taking the area under the graph.
Counting graph area below the displacement axis as positive work.

topics.name: Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem
topics.summary: Kinetic energy is the energy a body has because of its motion: \(KE=\tfrac12mv^2\). It is a scalar and can never be negative, because \(v^2\) is positive whichever way the body moves. Since it depends on the square of the speed, doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large. Kinetic energy and momentum are linked by \(KE=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}\), so two bodies with equal momentum do not have equal kinetic energy unless their masses are equal. The work-energy theorem says that the NET work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy: \(W_{net}=\tfrac12mv^2-\tfrac12mu^2\). The net work is the sum of the work of EVERY force acting, including friction, gravity and air resistance, each taken with its correct sign. Positive net work speeds a body up, negative net work slows it down, and zero net work (as in uniform circular motion or motion at constant velocity) leaves the speed unchanged. Because braking work must remove \(\tfrac12mu^2\), the stopping distance under a fixed braking force grows as the square of the initial speed.
topics.worked_example:
A block at rest on a rough floor is pushed through 5 m by a 10 N horizontal force; friction is 4 N.

Work by the push: \(+10\times5=50\) J.

Work by friction: \(-4\times5=-20\) J.

\(W_{net}=50-20=30\) J, so the block gains 30 J of kinetic energy, not 50 J.
common_mistakes: Equating the work of one named force (usually the applied force) to \(\Delta KE\) and ignoring friction or gravity.
Using \(\tfrac12m(v-u)^2\) instead of \(\tfrac12m\left(v^2-u^2\right)\).
Leaving out the factor \(\tfrac12\), or forgetting the final square root when solving for the speed.
Writing a negative kinetic energy; only the change \(\Delta KE\) can be negative.
Assuming equal momentum means equal kinetic energy.

topics.name: Potential Energy and Conservation of Mechanical Energy
topics.summary: Potential energy is stored energy that depends on position or shape. Near the Earth's surface the gravitational potential energy is \(PE=mgh\), measured from a chosen zero level; it increases when a body rises and decreases when it falls. A spring stretched or compressed by \(x\) stores \(U=\tfrac12kx^2\), which is never negative because \(x\) is squared. Potential energy can be defined only for conservative forces such as gravity and the spring force. Their work depends only on the end points, is zero around any closed path, and satisfies \(\Delta PE=-W_{conservative}\). Friction and air resistance are non-conservative: their work depends on the path length and turns mechanical energy into heat. The total mechanical energy \(KE+PE\) stays constant ONLY when every force doing work is conservative, which is why problems must say frictionless or smooth before you use \(mgh=\tfrac12mv^2\). When friction is present, mechanical energy is not conserved, and the energy lost equals the initial mechanical energy minus the final mechanical energy. Always use the stated value of \(g\).
topics.worked_example:
A 2 kg block starts from rest 5 m above the bottom of a rough incline and arrives with a speed of 8 m/s (\(g=10\) m/s\(^2\)).

Initial mechanical energy: \(mgh=2\times10\times5=100\) J.

Final mechanical energy: \(\tfrac12\times2\times8^2=64\) J.

Energy lost to friction \(=100-64=36\) J. On a smooth incline the speed would have been 10 m/s.
common_mistakes: Applying plain conservation of mechanical energy to a problem in which friction or air resistance is explicitly present.
Getting the sign of \(\Delta PE=mgh\) backwards, for example saying potential energy decreases while a body rises.
Treating spring energy as negative for compression, or forgetting the factor \(\tfrac12\) in \(\tfrac12kx^2\).
Using the full height instead of the difference in height between two points.
Believing the final speed of a projectile depends on the launch angle when only gravity acts.

topics.name: Power
topics.summary: Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred. The average power over a time \(t\) is \(P_{avg}=\dfrac Wt\), and the instantaneous power delivered by a force is the dot product \(P=\vec F\cdot\vec v=Fv\cos\theta\). Like work, power is a scalar with a sign: it is positive when the force has a component along the velocity, zero when the force is perpendicular to the velocity (a centripetal force, or gravity at the top of a projectile's path), and negative when the force opposes the motion, as friction does. A vehicle moving at constant velocity has zero NET power, yet its engine still delivers \(P=Fv\), where \(F\) balances the resistive forces. The SI unit is the watt, equal to one joule per second; one horsepower is about 746 W. The kilowatt-hour is a unit of ENERGY, not power: \(1\ \text{kWh}=3.6\times10^6\) J. Real machines waste some energy, so efficiency is output power divided by input power, times 100%. The output is always smaller than the input, so the input is found by dividing the output by the efficiency.
topics.worked_example:
A pump raises 200 kg of water through 9 m in 10 s and is 90% efficient (\(g=10\) m/s\(^2\)).

Useful work: \(mgh=200\times10\times9=18000\) J.

Output power: \(\dfrac{18000}{10}=1800\) W.

Input power: \(\dfrac{1800}{0.9}=2000\) W.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the output by the efficiency to get the input, instead of dividing.
Ignoring \(\cos\theta\) in \(P=Fv\cos\theta\), or giving positive power to a force that opposes the velocity.
Saying the engine power is zero at constant velocity because the net force is zero.
Confusing average power \(\dfrac Wt\) with the instantaneous power at the end of the interval.
Treating the kilowatt-hour as a unit of power.

topics.name: Collisions: Elastic and Inelastic, in One and Two Dimensions
topics.summary: A collision is a short, strong interaction between two bodies. If no external force acts, the total linear momentum is conserved in EVERY collision. What happens to kinetic energy decides the type. In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. In an inelastic collision only momentum is conserved; part of the kinetic energy becomes heat, sound and deformation. In a perfectly inelastic collision the bodies stick together and the loss is the largest possible. The coefficient of restitution \(e\) is the relative speed of separation divided by the relative speed of approach: \(e=1\) is elastic, \(0<e<1\) is partially inelastic and \(e=0\) is perfectly inelastic. A ball dropped from height \(h\) rebounds to \(e^2h\). In a one-dimensional elastic collision the velocities are simply exchanged ONLY when the masses are equal; for unequal masses the full formulas must be used. In two dimensions momentum is a vector, so it must be conserved separately along x and along y. When a body strikes an identical body at rest elastically and not head-on, the two move off at \(90^\circ\) to each other.
key_formulas: \(p_x\) and \(p_y\) conserved separately in two dimensions
topics.worked_example:
A 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s makes a head-on elastic collision with a 1 kg ball at rest.

\(v_1'=\dfrac{(2-1)\times3}{3}=1\) m/s and \(v_2'=\dfrac{2\times2\times3}{3}=4\) m/s.

Momentum check: \(2\times1+1\times4=6\) kg m/s, as before.

Energy check: \(1+8=9\) J, as before. A simple exchange (0 and 3 m/s) would conserve momentum but leave only 4.5 J, so it is wrong here.
common_mistakes: Assuming kinetic energy is conserved in an inelastic or perfectly inelastic collision.
Using the velocities-exchange shortcut when the two masses are not equal.
Carrying energy conservation straight through a sticking collision (for example in a ballistic pendulum) instead of using momentum for that step.
In two dimensions, conserving only one component of momentum or adding momenta as plain scalars.
Forgetting to give opposite velocities opposite signs in the momentum equation.
Using \(e\) instead of \(e^2\) for the rebound height.

Both develop the same power because the work is the same
Asha develops half the power of Bina
Asha develops twice the power of Bina
questions.explanation:
Both do the same work \(W=mgh\).

\(P=\dfrac{W}{t}\), so power is inversely proportional to time.

Asha takes half the time, so she develops twice the power.
questions.hint: Same work, less time means more power.
distractor_logic: Inverted the dependence of power on time
Confused work with power; equal work in different times means different power
Inverted the dependence of power on time

questions.question: In any collision between two bodies on which no external force acts, the quantity that is always conserved is
options: both the total kinetic energy and the speed of each body
neither momentum nor any form of energy
questions.explanation:

Kinetic energy is conserved only in the special case of an elastic collision.

questions.question: A collision in which the total kinetic energy is conserved along with the total momentum is called

Inelastic collision: only momentum is conserved; some kinetic energy is converted into other forms.

questions.question: For a perfectly inelastic collision, the coefficient of restitution \(e\) is
questions.explanation:

the mass of the lighter body to the mass of the heavier body

only as a sum of the speeds multiplied by the masses, without regard to direction
only perpendicular to the original direction of motion
separately along each of the two perpendicular axes

questions.question: A puck sliding on smooth ice makes an elastic collision, not head-on, with an identical puck at rest. The angle between the velocities of the two pucks after the collision is
questions.explanation:
Momentum: \(\vec u=\vec v_1+\vec v_2\) (equal masses). Kinetic energy: \(u^2=v_1^2+v_2^2\).

questions.explanation:

questions.explanation:
Rectangle (0 to 4 m): \(6\times4=24\) J.

The line crosses zero at \(x=6\) m. Triangle above the axis (4 m to 6 m): \(+\tfrac12\times2\times6=+6\) J.

Triangle below the axis (6 m to 8 m): \(-\tfrac12\times2\times6=-6\) J.

questions.explanation:
Lifting: gravity opposes the displacement, \(W=-mgh=-10\times10\times2=-200\) J.

Horizontal carry: gravity is perpendicular to the displacement, \(W=0\).

Lowering: gravity is along the displacement, \(W=+200\) J.

Total \(=-200+0+200=0\) J.

questions.explanation:

\(W=\tfrac12\times100\times(0.09-0.01)=50\times0.08=4\) J.

questions.explanation:

\(W=mgd\cos60^\circ=2\times10\times5\times\tfrac12=50\) J.

questions.explanation:

\(v=4\) m/s.

questions.explanation:
For one plank: \(F\,t=\tfrac12mu^2\), where \(t\) is the plank thickness.

Doubling the speed gives four times the kinetic energy.

The same force must act over four times the distance, that is 4 planks.

questions.explanation:
Work by the pull: \(20\times5\times0.8=80\) J.

Work by friction: \(-6\times5=-30\) J. Gravity and the normal force do no work.

\(W_{net}=50\) J \(=\tfrac12\times4\times v^2\), so \(v^2=25\) and \(v=5\) m/s.

distractor_logic: Ignored friction and equated the pull's work alone to the kinetic energy
Used the full 20 N for the pull instead of its horizontal component

questions.question: A particle of mass \(m\) moves with constant speed \(v\) in a circle of radius \(r\). The net work done on it during half a revolution is
questions.explanation:
The speed is constant, so \(\Delta KE=0\).

By the work-energy theorem \(W_{net}=\Delta KE=0\).

This agrees with the net (centripetal) force being perpendicular to the velocity at every instant.

distractor_logic: Multiplied the centripetal force \(\dfrac{mv^2}{r}\) by the path length \(\pi r\), ignoring that it is perpendicular to the motion

questions.explanation:
\(W_{net}=\Delta KE=\tfrac12\times1\times8^2-0=32\) J.

\(W_{air}=W_{net}-W_{gravity}=32-50=-18\) J.

distractor_logic: Gave a positive sign although air resistance opposes the motion

questions.explanation:
The surface is smooth, so \(\tfrac12mv^2=\tfrac12kx^2\).

\(\tfrac12\times2\times16=16\) J \(=\tfrac12\times800\times x^2\).

\(x^2=0.04\), so \(x=0.2\) m.

questions.question: A pendulum of length 1.6 m is pulled aside until the string makes \(60^\circ\) with the vertical and is released from rest. Ignoring air resistance and taking \(g=10\) m/s\(^2\), the speed of the bob at the lowest point is
questions.explanation:
Height fallen: \(h=L(1-\cos60^\circ)=1.6\times\tfrac12=0.8\) m.

The tension is perpendicular to the motion and does no work, so \(mgh=\tfrac12mv^2\).

\(v^2=2\times10\times0.8=16\), so \(v=4\) m/s.

distractor_logic: Took the height fallen as the full string length 1.6 m

questions.explanation:
Initial spring energy: \(\tfrac12kx^2=\tfrac12\times100\times0.04=2\) J.

Final kinetic energy \(=1.5\) J.

Energy dissipated \(=2-1.5=0.5\) J.

distractor_logic: Applied plain conservation of mechanical energy although the floor is rough

questions.explanation:
Energy just before impact: \(mg\times10\).

Energy after impact: \(0.8\times mg\times10=mg\times8\).

On the way up, mechanical energy is conserved, so \(mgh'=mg\times8\) and \(h'=8\) m.
questions.hint: 80% of the energy remains after the bounce.
distractor_logic: Used the 20% that was lost instead of the 80% that remains
Ignored the energy lost in the impact
Applied the 20% loss twice

questions.question: A stone is thrown at 20 m/s from the top of a 25 m high tower at some unknown angle to the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance and taking \(g=10\) m/s\(^2\), the speed with which it strikes the ground is
options: impossible to find without the angle of projection
questions.explanation:
Only gravity does work, so \(\tfrac12mu^2+mgh=\tfrac12mv^2\).

\(v^2=u^2+2gh=400+2\times10\times25=900\).

\(v=30\) m/s, whatever the launch angle.
questions.hint: Energy conservation does not care about the launch direction.
distractor_logic: Energy is a scalar, so the final speed does not depend on the direction of launch
Counted only the energy gained in the fall and ignored the initial kinetic energy
Added the speeds instead of adding the energies

questions.question: A stone is thrown vertically upward (no air resistance). It passes a point at height \(h\) once on the way up and once on the way down. Which statement is correct?
options: Its kinetic energy is greater on the way down
Its kinetic energy at height \(h\) is the same on the way up and on the way down
Its kinetic energy is greater on the way up
Its potential energy at height \(h\) is negative on the way down
questions.explanation:
Total mechanical energy \(E\) is conserved. At height \(h\), \(PE=mgh\) both times.

So \(KE=E-mgh\) is the same on the way up and on the way down; only the direction of the velocity differs.
questions.hint: Potential energy depends only on the height.
distractor_logic: Assumed gravity adds net energy during the fall; it only returns what it took on the way up

questions.explanation:

Input \(=\dfrac{\text{output}}{\text{efficiency}}=\dfrac{1800}{0.9}=2000\) W.

questions.explanation:

\(P=Fv=6000\times10=60000\) W \(=60\) kW.

questions.explanation:
Work done \(=Pt=16\times4=64\) J.

\(\tfrac12mv^2=64\), so \(v^2=\dfrac{2\times64}{2}=64\).

\(v=8\) m/s.

questions.explanation:

\(P_{avg}=\dfrac{900}{3}=300\) W, half of the final instantaneous power \(mgv=600\) W.

questions.question: A 3 kg body starts from rest on a smooth floor under a constant net force of 6 N. At the instant its kinetic energy is 24 J, the power delivered by the force is
questions.explanation:
\(\tfrac12\times3\times v^2=24\), so \(v^2=16\) and \(v=4\) m/s.

\(P=Fv=6\times4=24\) W.
questions.hint: Get the speed from the kinetic energy, then use \(P=Fv\).
distractor_logic: Used the acceleration value 2 m/s\(^2\) in place of the speed
Used a speed of 8 m/s, obtained by halving \(v^2=16\) instead of taking its square root
Multiplied the force by the kinetic energy

questions.question: A 1 kg block is released from rest at the top of a smooth curved ramp of height 1.25 m. At the bottom it moves onto a rough horizontal floor where the friction force is 2.5 N. Taking \(g=10\) m/s\(^2\), the distance it slides on the floor before stopping is
questions.explanation:
Smooth ramp: \(KE\) at the bottom \(=mgh=1\times10\times1.25=12.5\) J.

Rough floor: friction's work \(-2.5\times d\) removes this kinetic energy.

\(d=\dfrac{12.5}{2.5}=5\) m.
questions.hint: Conservation on the smooth ramp, work-energy theorem on the rough floor.
distractor_logic: Used \(mv^2=25\) J for the kinetic energy, leaving out the factor \(\tfrac12\)
Halved the energy available at the bottom
Assumed the block slides a distance equal to the ramp height

questions.question: A 2 kg block slides from rest down a frictionless ramp of height 0.45 m and, on the smooth level floor, collides head-on with a 1 kg block at rest. The coefficient of restitution is 0.5 and \(g=10\) m/s\(^2\). The speed of the 1 kg block just after the collision is
questions.explanation:
Speed at the bottom: \(u=\sqrt{2\times10\times0.45}=3\) m/s.

Momentum: \(2v_1'+v_2'=6\). Restitution: \(v_2'-v_1'=0.5\times3=1.5\).

Solving: \(v_1'=1.5\) m/s and \(v_2'=3\) m/s.
questions.hint: Energy conservation on the ramp, then momentum and \(e\) for the collision.

Treated the collision as perfectly inelastic (\(e=0\))
